title: I built a rally game with Claude and Three.js. Now I'm considering moving it to a real game engine. Looking for advice.
author: Conscious-Desk6823
selftext:
Hey everyone!

I'm an art director by trade, not a developer. A while ago, I started messing around with Claude and a super basic 2D canvas rally game, just to see what was possible.

One thing led to another, and it slowly turned into Over The Edge, an isometric 3D rally game running entirely in the browser.

It's inspired by the old Colin McRae games I used to love as a kid. But playing it recently on an arcade machine I bought, I was thinking what would make this game even better. 😛. So I focused more on arcade fun, high-speed chases, pushing friends off cliffs, and stages that seem determined to mess with you.

**What started as a vibe coding experiment has become a pretty personal project.**

To be transparent, Claude has done most of the coding, with some additional help from a developer friend. My role has mainly been art direction, visual references, creative decisions, and countless rounds of testing and iteration.

**Some of the things I've managed to get working with Claude:**

* Procedurally generated stages across four countries, with seeded roads, environments, and weather.
* Cars generated entirely through code, using real blueprints as visual references.
* Dynamic dirt and damage systems using custom shaders.
* A first, very rough version of a track editor.
* AI opponents, online multiplayer lobbies, and a progression system. (the AI is actually quite fun to play against)

**But it's still pretty wonky.**

The car models need work, the soundscape is very basic, and I'm running into performance and optimization challenges. There's still a lot to figure out. (If there's a 3d modeler out there please let me know!)

**And that's where I'm looking for some advice.**

I've been pushing the Three.js version pretty far, and I'm starting to feel its limitations. (I had to scale back the fanciness quite a bit. That why I'm now seriously considering moving to a dedicated game engine to take the project further. (more stages, more details, etc etc)

**A few things I'm curious about:**

* **Procedural generation:** The entire game currently generates its roads, environments, and car geometry at runtime using JavaScript. How would you approach something like this in Godot? Can the same principles carry over, or would I need to rethink the system?
* **Choosing an engine:** Would Godot be a good fit for a game like this, or would Unity or Unreal offer significantly more possibilities, particularly for larger environments, physics, and visual effects?
* **Is there still a place for games like this?** With so many racing games focused on realism and simulation, I'm curious whether people still enjoy more accessible, slightly chaotic arcade rally games, especially ones built around having fun with friends.

I'm not pretending this is some finished indie masterpiece. It's a passion project that has grown way beyond what I originally imagined, and I'm trying to figure out the smartest way forward.

If anyone wants to see what I'm working with, the current browser version is here:

[https://overtheedge.app](https://overtheedge.app/)

The game is completely free to play. This is really just a passion project, and I'm mainly looking for feedback before deciding where to take it next and make something more serious out of this. 😱

If someone is interested I can share a more detailed use case about what the design decisions were. 

*Small note to the mods: I originally tried sharing an earlier version of this case study from a brand-new Reddit account, but it was automatically removed by Reddit's filters. I contacted the moderators but haven't heard back, so I'm sharing this revised version from my original account. Happy to adjust anything if needed!*

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body: If you're running into performance issues on a 3d game using ThreeJS, Godot is not going to make things much better. Honestly I'd argue ThreeJS  might be more performant at its base than Godot. AI can help you optimize it, but Godot's inherent optimizations for physics, lighting, etc in 3d is utterly horrible at its base. You're much better using Unity in this particular case, which could support hundreds of cars in a far more complex environment without blinking. If you're willing to let AI tinker with the Godot source and completely rewrite areas of the code (though likely to be things you'll have to iron the bugs out of over time) then you can probably get away with it. But I think Unity would handle your issues out of the box as long as you just instruct your AI to keep an eye out for available optimizations as you go. To use ECS/DOTS and other frameworks Unity specifically implemented for that purpose. Etc.

replies.author: Conscious-Desk6823
replies.body: That's exactly what I'm looking for! I have been tinkering with Unity back when I was in school, but havent dared opening it since then. 😅You think Unity could handle live track generation? I would love to keep that feature.

replies.author: ThisGuyCrohns
replies.body: Not really. Godot can use cpp. Godot can have incredible performance if you know what you’re doing. People need to stop using high level languages if you want performance

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body: This isn't about C++ vs Gscript. Their physics and lighting engine for 3d scenes is terrible. it's getting better, but it's still terrible. They've been trying to make it look better but optimization was left along the wayside. They're the GOAT for 2d, but not remotely for 3d. I'd rather pick up  Unity or Unreal and have an engine with physics/lighting/rendering/etc for 3d all with extreme levels of optimization built in. Entire systems dedicated to rendering hundreds or thousands or more of physics objects simultaneously without any slowdown. Rather than being forced to rewrite those frameworks. Like great, Godot is open source, you CAN customize it however you want. Doesn't mean it's not time consuming to do so and leaves you reinventing the wheel. You're frankly better off just building your own engine from scratch if going for 3d than using Godot.

replies.author: cratercamper
replies.body:
Claude is sometimes reluctant to do bigger chunks of work if it thinks it can steer you away from it. This can also be partially caused by them thinking there are your rulings which are in fact not meant like that by you - so it is worth to discuss the assumptions.   
  
Also cheap (your attention, not tokens) is letting Claude rewrite something - you just tell it it should have the same results, but that it internally should do it differently.

Also let Claude build system for performance analysis - it should be able to measure every single detail in your game. Do this as multistep - first let it measure all parts of the game and then dive more and more into parts that Claude will say are not absolutely minimal already.

comments.author: Omzy
comments.body: Do not move this to another engine, roll it into your own engine. This is the big brain move. Games like this do much better with a lean engine created just for them, and your game already works. Just ask Claude to pitch a plan to move the game into its own engine as a desktop app, to make a system by system plan to optimize it. It will analyze where the worst performance is and fix the worst offenders and your game will be higher quality, closer to release, and still on a full AI pipeline if you do this. Claude is more than capable of building every piece of any game engine out there (including Unreal) if you but just know what pieces to ask for. All you have to know is what pieces your game is missing, like instanced meshes for example, ask Claude to add it to your engine, it will go through the white papers and have it done in 5 minutes. Source: i did this with my Game and it was a mind expanding game changer. Never going back to a one size fits all engine.

replies.author: thefunkybassist
replies.body:
The main thing is VRAM+high bandwidth. Your GPU has high memory bandwith but 16Gb isn't that much for a LLM. You could try running Qwen 3.8 27B IQ4\_XS with CPU offloading which will be slower, or a smaller Qwen version.

3d modeling even with frontier models does oversight or a solid plan. I had to spend quite some time directing Claude how to fix overlaps for example, it started messing up the whole production because of overcomplication.

And prepare to need some time to get any LLM up and running in a stable way, with a config that works best for you. It took me many months before I got a stable setup that doesn't loop, constantly throws vague errors, etc.

replies.author: Omzy
replies.body: That comes with experience and study. There's no shortcut to experience. The easiest way to answer that is, ask yourself, is there something 'not right' or 'off' about the experience? Then ask others the same question and they will tell you what's missing. You can also watch videos about engine tech, like material shaders, optimization techniques, lighting techniques and what other engines do to try to understand what is still missing. You'll find that adding only a few simple things can take your game from barely palatable to AA quality. But again, there is no substitute for learning and experience. A fancier engine won't paper over that either--in fact it will make it worse as you will not understand how to properly use the tech and will make much costlier mistakes. Better to start simple and build up your knowledge base piece by piece.

ask ai to profile it, and always ground decisions in data and spike solutions. if you don't know any area of expertise - reason with it. asking even the simplest "how do we do this more intelligently? also retro your agents work if they don't progress through issues for a significant time (eg. matt pocock /retro or roll your own)

replies.author: Jedi_sephiroth
replies.body: Yeah and how many iterations did it take for those animations? What is your work flow?'

replies.author: stumperkoek
replies.body:
The first 3 animations were 90% correct on first go. After 1 extra prompt those got fixed. My remarks for the fixes were similar for those 3. The next 3 animations were correct in 1 go, it also prompted as one of the steps that it took the feedback on the first 3 into account and solved/prevented te same issues for those animations.

For my workflow: I work with Unity and downloaded a reference T-pose with skeleton and skin from Mixamo. Then I found some animations from Mixamo that I liked and downloaded those without skin, just animation clips only. Claude build the animator around my character controller using those animations.
Then I prompted that some animations were missing (I had a standing up animation if the character fell face down, but couldn't find a good one for standing up when the character fell and ended up face up). I asked to look at the face down animation and make a face up animation of the same length, with the same speed for getting up. It then build a animation by importing the reference rig into Blender and key framing the animation. It did an extra pass for checking body parts clipping through the floor or other body parts. Animations was perfect in one go.

For another animation (entering a pickup truck) it imported the pickup truck model, analyzed how far the door could open and then made an animation where the player finds the door handle, opens the door, steps on the step up bar thingy and takes a seat. Since my truck has a front and back seat and those doors differ in size, it made it with Inverse Kinematics, so the character finds the width of the door frame and places it hands accordingly. The first pass of this was 90% correct, with 1 foot clipping throught the other leg and the seat slightly. After one additional prompt that got changed. If you play frame by frame it is still not 100% there, but in real time play it is not noticable. I asked some play testers about the animations and not one of them noticed it.

comments.author: TrickyPistachio
comments.body:
\> Is there still a place for games like this?

This is the only thing I can really give feedback on, which is to say this is a great game regardless of AI involvement. The looks are fun and clean, with cool dust and weather effects. The feel is so good, from the driving to the collisions and destructible pieces; the little car's body weight shunting around. Good stuff. It's got that dangerous precision feel of rally racers too, that's probably what I really like here; you're not just wafting around a safe track. But at the same time there are jumps and puddles and sheep and people to honk at and run over, so it feels like it's worth paying attention but still gives you lots of fun gamey moments.

So my feedback is that it's very good and very clean, but it wants some juice. As it is I would buy it, but I'd be sad for it not stepping up to the next level of potential it has. 

For example, have you considered music? I imagine to myself your game with this playing:

[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CV9aHyVXSrw](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CV9aHyVXSrw)

I'd love to be racing and perfecting my fastest times on those really fun tracks with music amping me up as I go, not just driving a well-produced, clean racer.

What if it has a bunch of real life (still in the cute isometric style) track layouts? That would get some attention I think.

Or what if it does the whole co-driver narration? Could be serious like Dirt Rally, or arcadey fun like Sega Rally.

Oh I just noticed the little Stratos!!! SO GOOD!

That's all I got. 😄 Fantastic game. I haven't played many of this mini-rally genre, but of the few I've tried, this is better.

comments.author: nekomnia
comments.body:
Three.js CAN be a game engine, seriously.

I worked for an AI game engine & agent company, which is targeting web-based game creation. What they're using as the foundation? Three.js. Why? It provides a unified source of truth and a lean language to work on, which is pretty friendly for agents. And also, the performance ceiling of Three.js are pretty high.

What the developers need are "the suitable", not "the best". From my observation, what really needed here is a good debugging and feedback loop, assets, and gameplay refinement. Godot, Unity etc. doesn't automatically solves this, if not creating more learning curve and debts.

That being said, if you really want an editor, sibling web-based stacks like Babylon.js or PlayCanvas are potentially good options.

Cheers and good luck on your dev journey.

comments.author: Still_Explorer
comments.body:
If you know about the game "CrossCode" this was made with HTML5 and Javascript technologies but was baked into an executable.

Since you have the entire game (and hence the game engine) up and running it would be clever idea to retain it as it is.

Note that it wouldn't be a bad idea the game to be ported to Unreal6 or Unity, only that there's a chance that something will be "lost" in translation. Probably might happen, or probably not. But essentially the point is that the game will be used as a reference but will have to be refurbished from scratch to the new engine. Only this is my concern, but if you are very positive about it then go for it.

So in order to capture what you have now, you might try to do some repackacing test and if you are happy with it to continue with this idea:

Either you use Tauri  
[https://v1.tauri.app/v1/guides/getting-started/setup/html-css-js/](https://v1.tauri.app/v1/guides/getting-started/setup/html-css-js/)

Also some other optional

Direct Comparison of Options

|Method|Performance|Final Build Size|Setup Complexity|Best For|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|Tauri|🔥 Excellent (Uses system Webview)|📦 Tiny (\~10–20 MB)|Mid-High (Requires Rust setup)|Production games, fast loading, small downloads.|
|Electron|⚡ Good (Includes dedicated Chromium)|🐘 Large (\~100+ MB)|🟢 Very Easy (Pure JavaScript)|Quick prototypes, seamless Steam API integration.|
|NW.js|⚡ Good (Chromium-based)|🐘 Large (\~100+ MB)|🟢 Very Easy (Legacy friendly)|Source protection (compiles JS to native bytecode).|
